title: NY State Senate · District 31
area: Northern Manhattan: Washington Heights, Inwood, and Marble Hill, extending south through Hamilton Heights, Morningside Heights, the Upper West Side, Hell's Kitchen, and Chelsea.

context.text: Incumbent Robert Jackson defeated Nayma Silver-Matos in the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary, 71.9% to 27.7%. He also advanced on the Working Families Party line, which was uncontested. As of this writing, no Republican or other opposition candidate has filed for the general election, leaving Jackson unopposed on the ballot.

summary.text: Robert Jackson is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for re-election to New York State Senate District 31, covering Washington Heights, Inwood, and other northern and west Manhattan neighborhoods. First elected to the Senate in 2018 after 12 years on the New York City Council, he chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee and is unopposed in the general election.

background.text: Attended New York City public schools, including P.S. 186 in Washington Heights and Benjamin Franklin High School in the Bronx, and graduated from the State University of New York at New Paltz.

As a Community School Board president, filed and won a lawsuit (Campaign for Fiscal Equity v. State of New York) arguing that the state's school-funding formula shortchanged New York City students; walked 150 miles to Albany to draw attention to the case, which resulted in a court-ordered increase in city school funding.

Served on the New York City Council from 2002 to 2013, representing the 7th District in Manhattan, including as Chair of the Council's Education Committee and co-chair of the Black, Latino, and Asian Caucus.
Has served as a Democratic District Leader in Manhattan since 2015.
Elected to the State Senate in 2018, defeating incumbent Marisol Alcantara in the Democratic primary; re-elected in 2020, 2022, and 2024.

priorities.text: Workers' rights and job creation, including support for small businesses.
Gun violence reduction and public safety.
Immigrant services and maintaining community services such as senior centers and libraries.

positions.summary: Sponsored S10687, which would require additional tenant notice before landlords can seek major capital improvement rent increases.

record.text: Sponsored S10655, implementing a state collective-bargaining agreement covering more than 56,000 Professional, Scientific and Technical Services Unit employees; passed the Senate 60–0 on June 4, 2026 and signed by the Governor June 12, 2026 (Chapter 133).

Sponsored S10605, extending from 2026 to 2030 the deadline for retirement-system members and workers'-compensation claimants to file World Trade Center rescue, recovery, or cleanup-related disability claims; passed the Senate 61–0 on June 2, 2026 and signed by the Governor September 10, 2026 (Chapter 296).

Sponsored S10590, restoring a 55-years-old/30-years-of-service retirement option and lowering the normal retirement age from 63 to 62 for uniformed court officers and peace officers in the Unified Court System; passed the Senate 61–0 on June 2, 2026 and was delivered to the Governor.
Voted no on S8455-B, which places new restrictions on the sale of flare guns; the bill passed the Senate 35–25 on June 1, 2026.
Voted yes on S9500-A, establishing the New York State Grid Reliability and Energy Affordability Transition Program; passed the Senate 39–21 on June 1, 2026.
Chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee in the 2025–2026 session and also sits on the Education, Health, Housing, Higher Education, and Labor committees.
